Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• 48-year-old man with asthma presents with 3 days of watery diarrhoea (every ~10 min), central abdominal cramps relieved after stool, one episode of vomiting, mild nausea, no visible blood, uncertain low-grade fever, mild central tenderness on self-palpation.  
• Not drinking adequately; no red-flag features (no severe pain, no persistent vomiting with blood, no chest pain, no dyspnoea beyond baseline, no peritonism).  
• Father died of colorectal cancer.  

Working diagnosis  
• Acute infectious gastroenteritis – likely viral (high likelihood): abrupt onset, self-limited course, diarrhoea + brief vomiting, absence of systemic toxicity or blood. Supported by DDx model.  

Considerations  
• Bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis (medium likelihood).  
• Post-infectious or functional diarrhoea/IBS if symptoms persist (low-medium).  
• Inflammatory bowel disease or colorectal malignancy considered low probability at this stage given acute presentation but flagged due to family history.  

Management  
• Symptomatic care: oral rehydration advised; monitor for fever, bloody stool, increasing pain, or persistent vomiting.  
• Avoid antibiotics unless clinical picture changes.  
• Safety-net: attend in-person GP review if symptoms worsen or no improvement within 24–48 h.  

Health Promotion & Planning

- Education on chronic disease prevention and lifestyle modification:  Advised increased fluid intake and rest; counselled on signs that warrant urgent review. Broader preventive education not recorded.  
- Patient health goals and priorities:  Wishes to recover and return to work; concerned about risk of bowel cancer.  
- Eligibility for GP Management Plan (GPMP) or Team Care Arrangements (TCA):  Not discussed.  
- Referrals (allied health, Quitline, AOD services, Aboriginal health worker, or social supports):  Plan for in-person GP review if no improvement.  
- Follow-up and recall appointments scheduled:  Patient to self-monitor; advised GP review within 1–2 days if symptoms persist or worsen.  

Consider

- Mental health support or counselling referral:  Not recorded (consider if anxiety persists).  
- Specialist referral for complex chronic disease management:  Not required currently; possible future gastroenterology referral if chronic bowel symptoms or screening due to family history.  
- Dental referral if oral health issues identified:  Not recorded.  
- Optometry referral for visual concerns or regular screening:  Not recorded.  
- Audiometry referral if hearing issues suspected:  Not recorded.  
- Social work or housing support referral if social determinants affect health:  Not recorded.  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Acute infectious gastroenteritis – likely viral (High): sudden watery diarrhoea, transient vomiting, mild abdominal cramps, no blood or high fever.  
2. Bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis (Medium): similar symptoms; uncertain food exposure; less supported by absence of fever/blood.  
3. Inflammatory bowel disease flare (Low): diarrhoea and pain, but very acute onset and lack of blood make this less likely.  

Quality checks

● Missing but clinically expected elements: no vital signs, BMI, immunisation review, diet/smoking/alcohol history, formal abdominal examination, baseline labs, FOBT screening given family history.  
● Internal conflicts: none noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality notes: patient audio clear; some hesitancy; age initially misstated then corrected; no objective examination possible via telehealth.
